sections.title: Learning a Class from Examples
rules: In supervised learning, a training set contains labeled examples.
Each example pairs an input vector with an output label.
Positive examples belong to the target class.
Negative examples do not belong to the target class.
We want to find a description that fits all positive examples.
The learned description must exclude all negative examples.
We define a hypothesis class as the set of candidate descriptions.
For a family car, we use price and engine power as input features.
A rectangle in feature space defines the hypothesis class.
The hypothesis function outputs one for positive examples and zero for negative examples.
The most specific hypothesis is the smallest rectangle enclosing all positive examples.
The most general hypothesis is the largest rectangle enclosing positive examples without negative examples.
The version space contains all hypotheses consistent with the training set.
The margin is the distance between the decision boundary and the nearest instances.
A hypothesis with the maximum margin provides better generalization on unseen data.

sections.title: Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) Dimension
rules: The VC dimension measures the capacity of a hypothesis class.
A dataset of N points allows two to the power of N distinct binary labelings.
A hypothesis class shatters a dataset if it can implement all possible labelings.
The VC dimension is the maximum number of points that the hypothesis class can shatter.
Axis-aligned rectangles in two dimensions shatter four points.
Axis-aligned rectangles cannot shatter any set of five points.
The VC dimension of axis-aligned rectangles in two dimensions is four.
The VC dimension does not depend on the probability distribution of the data.

sections.title: Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) Learning
rules: Leslie Valiant introduced Probably Approximately Correct learning.
In PAC learning, epsilon is the error tolerance.
The parameter delta is the probability of failure.
The learner must find a hypothesis with error less than epsilon.
The guarantee must hold with probability at least one minus delta.
We calculate the required sample size N from epsilon and delta.
Sample complexity increases when you decrease epsilon.
Sample complexity increases when you decrease delta.
PAC learning gives distribution-free sample size bounds for hypothesis classes.

sections.title: Noise
rules: Noise is any unwanted anomaly in the data.
Incorrect sensor readings cause noise in input values.
Human errors cause noise in teacher labels.
Hidden and unobserved variables also act as noise.
Noise makes class separation difficult with simple hypotheses.
Complex hypotheses can fit noise and cause poor generalization.
Occam's razor states that we must prefer simpler models.
A simpler model with small training error generalizes better than an overly complex model.

sections.title: Learning Multiple Classes
rules: In multiclass learning, each instance belongs to one of K classes.
We encode target labels as one-of-K binary vectors.
The target vector contains a single one and K minus one zeros.
We train K separate discriminant functions for the K classes.
The classifier assigns an input to the class with the highest score.
An ambiguity region occurs when two classes yield the same highest score.
In ambiguous regions, the classifier can reject the decision.
Rejection prevents costly classification errors.

sections.title: Regression
rules: Regression predicts a continuous numeric output from input features.
We assume the target value equals a deterministic function plus zero-mean random noise.
The model approximates the true function with parameters theta.
Linear regression models the output as a straight line.
The sum of squared errors measures the difference between actual targets and model outputs.
We calculate optimal parameters by minimizing the sum of squared errors.
The optimal line minimizes the vertical distances between data points and the regression line.

sections.title: Model Selection and Generalization
rules: Generalization measures model performance on new and unseen data.
Underfitting occurs when the model is too simple for the data.
Overfitting occurs when the model memorizes training noise.
Inductive bias represents the assumptions that allow a model to generalize.
We split available data into training, validation, and test sets.
The algorithm trains model parameters on the training set.
The user selects model complexity and hyperparameters on the validation set.
The test set evaluates the final generalization error.
Cross-validation rotates data folds to evaluate models on small datasets.

sections.title: Dimensions of a Supervised Machine Learning Algorithm
rules: Three core dimensions define any supervised learning algorithm.
The first dimension is the model or hypothesis class.
The second dimension is the loss function that penalizes errors.
The third dimension is the optimization algorithm that minimizes the loss.
Linear models, neural networks, and decision trees represent different model classes.
Zero-one loss and squared error represent common loss functions.
Gradient descent and closed-form equations represent common optimization algorithms.
Choosing different combinations of these three dimensions produces different learning algorithms.

sections.title: Notes
rules: Tom Mitchell introduced version spaces and candidate elimination.
Vladimir Vapnik developed statistical learning theory and the VC dimension.
Leslie Valiant formulated PAC learning theory in nineteen eighty-four.
A machine learning algorithm must possess inductive bias to learn from finite data.
